extracted.intended_audience: poets, literary critics, and educated readers evaluating poetic diction and metre
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and critical principles for distinguishing the language, arrangement, and effects appropriate to metrical poetry versus prose, and for judging when metrical form succeeds or becomes mere ornament. Focuses on metre's origin, its required union with passion and will, appropriate diction, and pitfalls of prosaism or pseudo-poetry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Essential difference between prose and metrical composition
rubrics_metrics.description: There may be an essential difference between the language (construction, ordonnance, order) of prose and of metrical composition — not merely a difference of words, but of style, arrangement, and relative importance of parts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The burden of proof lies with anyone denying this; shared vocabulary does not imply identical style. Coleridge compares stanzas and conversational language to show that order and construction appropriate to prose may be disproportionate in verse. Opponents who point to prose-like lines in good poetry must still show that all or most poetic passages could suitably be prose; isolated neutral instances do not suffice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modes of expression appropriate to each genre
rubrics_metrics.description: There exist modes of expression, constructions, and orders of sentences which are fitting and natural in serious prose but would be disproportionate and heterogeneous in metrical poetry, and vice versa.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critique ought to ask whether particular expressions are naturally placed in prose or verse. Examples: certain sequences and sentence-orders in narration fit conversational prose better than the compact, subordinated arrangement expected in poetry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Origin of metre: balance of passion and will
rubrics_metrics.description: Metre originates in a mental balance effected to hold passion's workings in check; it becomes organized into metre by a voluntary act of will and judgment for the purpose of pleasure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understanding metre's origin helps explain its required characteristics (see related criteria). Metre is not purely spontaneous nor purely artificial but derives from interplay between emotion and conscious regulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Metre must be accompanied by the natural language of excitement
rubrics_metrics.description: Because the elements of metre owe their existence to a state of increased excitement, the metre itself should be accompanied by the natural language of that excitement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poetic diction should reflect the heightened feeling that generates metre; when the language does not show corresponding excitement the metrical effect is weakened or misplaced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discernible traces of present volition in metrical language
rubrics_metrics.description: As metre is formed artificially by voluntary act with the aim of blending delight and emotion, traces of present volition (the poet's conscious shaping) should be proportionally discernible throughout metrical language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poetry requires an interpenetration of spontaneous feeling and deliberate craft. The presence of deliberate organization—choices of arrangement, emphasis, and form—should be evident and not wholly concealed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Union/interpenetration of passion and will
rubrics_metrics.description: There must be a union — an interpenetration — of passion (spontaneous impulse) and will (conscious purpose) in metrical composition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This partnership must be present and reconciled; poetry that lacks this union risks either wild incoherence (too much spontaneity) or mechanical artifice (too much will).

rubrics_metrics.name: Greater frequency of picturesque and vivifying language in poetry
rubrics_metrics.description: Metrical composition tends to employ a greater frequency of forms and figures of speech—picturesque and vivifying language—than would be natural in prose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Figures originally offspring of passion become in poetry 'the adopted children of power.' The poet supplies the reader with a tacit compact that such increased figurative language is appropriate and pleasurable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Metre as stimulant of attention requires appropriate matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Metre acts as a stimulant to attention and increases vivacity and susceptibility through surprise and recurring curiosity; without appropriate subject-matter or thought the stimulation leads to disappointment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Metre can only enhance suitable material; if the thoughts or expressions are inadequate, the heightened attention aroused by metre will feel frustrated (analogy: leaping in the dark). Critics should judge whether metre's vivacity is matched by substantive content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Metre is not sufficient alone — it must combine with other poetic elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Metre by itself is like yeast: worthless or disagreeable alone but capable of vivifying the 'liquor' with which it is proportionally combined; it is insufficient as a sole poetic power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate metre in relation to diction, imagery, feeling, arrangement. Relying on metre alone (or treating metre as the only poetic distinction) is inadequate criticism and inadequate poetry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate metre in combination with other elements
rubrics_metrics.description: One must assess metre by the powers it exerts in combination with other elements of poetry (diction, imagery, arrangement), not in abstraction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coleridge faults attempts to treat metre's powers in isolation; critics should identify the other elements required for metre to produce pleasurable effects and examine their interaction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence of prose-verse neutral passages does not negate difference
rubrics_metrics.description: There are sentences and lines that would fit equally well in prose or verse, but their existence only shows overlap, not identity of the two registers in general.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include certain sonnet lines or well-written prose-like lines in poetry. Critics must distinguish between universal interchangeability (which is false) and occasional overlap (which is real).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid prosaism — prose-like diction in verse detracts from poetry
rubrics_metrics.description: Prosaisms (prose-like lines) detract from a poem's merits and may eventually make metre a feature only to the eye; in blank verse prosaisms can often be transcribed unchanged into prose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test whether lines can be rendered into prose without loss of meaning or effect; if so, the metrical form may be superficial. In rhyme, changing final words can reveal prosaism. Prosaism is a substantive fault distinct from mere neutrality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Style must be governed by grammar, logic, psychology, and taste
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet should regulate style by principles — grammar, logic, psychology, and the accumulated knowledge that constitutes taste; ignorance or neglect of these principles indicates incompetence, not genius.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These principles allow the poet to judge appropriate registers (e.g., suppressed vs indulged anger) by imagination informed by reason, not by crude imitation of vulgar speech. Taste arises from applied knowledge and disciplined practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rules of imagination are internal; poetry resists purely external rules
rubrics_metrics.description: The creative rules of poetry arise from the imagination itself; if poetry were reducible to external mechanical rules it would cease to be poetry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criticism should establish principles but avoid turning poetic composition into mere craft. The 'rules' are the formative powers of imagination and should guide rather than mechanically prescribe artistic creation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish genuine poetic fervour from pseudo-poetry
rubrics_metrics.description: Genuine poetic fervour (self-impassioned warmth and elevation) must be distinguished from pseudo-poetry—affectation, hysteric exertion, or contrived ornament—that simulates passion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use examples to discriminate: Donne's apostrophes can be authentic; odes to abstract terms or overwrought rhetorical flourishes often feel false. The poet's instinct and cultivated taste should expose 'changeling' artifices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of epithets and personification must be judged for sense and appropriateness
rubrics_metrics.description: Adjunction of epithets or mythological personifications may give a poetic cast but can be hackneyed, anachronistic, or convey incongruous imagery; faults may stem from bad sense rather than genre differences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether epithets (e.g., 'smiling mornings' or invoking Phoebus) add meaningful poetic effect or merely reflect worn schoolboy images. Consider historical context: what pleased earlier readers may strike modern readers as puerile.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeal to practice of the best poets as evidentiary standard
rubrics_metrics.description: The consistent practice of great poets across countries and ages provides authority for the opinion that there are essential differences between prose and metrical composition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When theoretical disputes arise, examine exemplars (Homer to Milton, Spenser, etc.) to see how poets handled diction, metre, and arrangement. Practice across tradition supports critical claims.
